name: Simple Web App
tagline: A monolith, a database and a cache — the starting point for most products
summary: A browser talks over HTTPS to a single backend application that reads and writes PostgreSQL. Redis stores sessions and hot lookups, and a CDN serves static assets so the application only handles dynamic requests.

nodes.label: Browser
nodes.why: Sends HTTPS requests for pages and JSON; nothing is pushed to it, so plain request/response is enough.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.why: JavaScript, CSS and images are served from edge locations close to the user and never reach the application server.

nodes.label: Web Application
nodes.why: One deployable unit is the fastest way to ship and debug while the team and traffic are small.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.why: Keeps login sessions out of the application's memory so any instance can serve any user, and caches hot reads with a TTL.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Relational data with constraints and transactions covers almost every early product; it is well understood and easy to host.

flows.name: Load a page
steps: The application checks the session cookie and looks up the product.
Redis is asked first; on a miss the application falls back to the database.
PostgreSQL returns the row, which is cached in Redis with a TTL and rendered.

flows.name: Fetch static assets
steps: The CDN serves them from the nearest edge; the origin is contacted only on a cache miss.

flows.name: Log in
steps: The browser POSTs credentials over HTTPS.
The application verifies the password hash.
A session is stored in Redis and its id is set as a cookie.

decisions.why: One codebase, one deployment and one database transaction boundary keep a small team fast. Most products never outgrow this.
decisions.tradeoff: Everything scales together and a bug anywhere can take the whole app down. Splitting later requires discipline about module boundaries now.

decisions.decision: Keep sessions in Redis instead of application memory
decisions.why: Any application instance can serve any request, so instances can restart or be added behind a load balancer without logging users out.
decisions.tradeoff: One more service to run and a hard dependency: if Redis is down, nobody is logged in. Storing sessions in PostgreSQL avoids the extra service but adds database load on every request.

decisions.why: Constraints, joins and transactions catch data errors early; JSONB covers semi-structured needs without a second store.
decisions.tradeoff: Schema changes need migrations and horizontal write scaling is hard — acceptable long before it becomes a real limit.

versions.title: App + database
versions.summary: The browser talks to one server that owns everything. Fine for a prototype and low traffic.

versions.title: Add Redis
versions.summary: Sessions move out of process and hot reads are cached, so the app can run as several identical instances.

versions.title: Add a CDN
versions.summary: Static assets leave the application server; the origin only sees dynamic requests.

textAlternative: A browser at the top sends HTTPS requests to a single web application in the middle and fetches static assets from a CDN on the left. The application reads and writes a PostgreSQL database at the bottom and uses Redis, to the right, for sessions and cached lookups.
